"Information Disorder and Its Threat to Democracy"
Please join us for a discussion on mis- dis- and mal-information and its threat to democracy with
Dr. Daniel Rogers, the Co-Founder and Executive Director at the Global Disinformation Index,
an NGO that aims to catalyze change in the tech industry to disincentivize the creation and
dissemination of online disinformation.
Date: Wednesday, January 5, 2022
Time: 1:00 - 2:00 p.m.
Meeting Link:
Dr. Rogers is a physicist, an author, and an expert in cryptography, cybercrime, disinformation,
and security. He currently teaches in the Cybercrime and Global Security Masters Program at
New York University and serves as a Technical Advisor for the United Nations Development
Programme. His presentation will highlight the complexities of defining disinformation and
discuss tangible ways to counter it.
This presentation is co-sponsored by the Office of Security and the Democracy, Human Rights,
and Governance Center within the Development, Democracy, and Innovation Bureau. The
session will be part of the quarterly SEC Guest Speaker Series which aims to help all USAID
staff better understand security-related issues impacting our work, and DDI/DRG's ongoing
work in this area, including the recently released USAID's Disinformation Primer.
Any questions concerning this information may be directed to Daniel Stolkowski
([contact omitted]) and Diana Parzik ([contact omitted])

Information Disorder
and Its Threat to
Democracy
Dr. Daniel J. Rogers
GDI
January 2022

We are at a Watershed Moment
in the History of Information.
The internet is one of the greatest agents of free
speech and democracy the world has ever seen. It
gives individuals and communities access to
unprecedented tools for self-expression, new platforms
to build communities, and new capabilities to speak
truth to power.
But the power of those tools threaten established
democracies, and social media is being corrupted,
exploited, and weaponized by those with the power to
control the flow of information and distort reality.
РПР 2ОС
IDEAS
ПЛАЙ
вЛАСТЬ

THE BAD GUYS ARE
WINNING
If the 20th century was the story of slow, uneven progress toward the
victory of liberal democracy over other idcologics-
-communism,
fascism, virulent nationalism—the 21 st century is, so far, a story of the
reverse.
By Anne Applebaum
Illustrations by Michael Houtz
GDI

This is 5th Generation Warfare.
"World War IIl is a guerrilla information war with no division between
military and civilian participation." - Marshall McLuhan, 1970
Disinformation, or adversarial narrative conflict, is an example of the kind of
networked conflict that comprises what Col. Richard Szapranski and David Axe have
called Fifth Generation Warfare.
Adversarial narratives are rooted in conflict or opposition between actors and their
interests, and especially between a social in-group and an out-group. When adversarial
narratives are deployed, they create a series of smaller conflicts played out across the
networked information environment that inflame social tensions and amplify perceived
grievances of individuals, groups and institutions.
GDI
Marshall
McLuhan
Culture Is
Our
Business

Social Media Provides
the Perfect Storm.
Information consumers tend to believe four things:
1) That which they see first
2) That which they see the most
3) That which comes from a source they trust
4) That which is not challenged by a rebuttal
Social media platforms, whose algorithms reward engagement
above all else, provide a perfect storm for disinformation peddlers
to achieve these four aims. Fact-checking and other true/false
determinations will always fail to keep pace with the most
aggressive manipulators exploiting social media for gain. Winning
in narrative conflict requires a new approach that rapidly identifies
and persistently outs the sources of disinformation.

How We Define Disinformation
• The definition of Disinformation must transcend these overly
simple false dichotomies.
GDI views disinformation through the lens of adversarial
narrative conflict. Adversarial narratives:
• Can be implicit or explicit;
• Are intentionally misleading;
Are adversarial against an at-risk individual or group, or an
institution like science, medicine, or democratically-elected
government;
Most importantly, create a risk of harm
• This definition transcends the morass of false binaries and
identifies disinformation explicitly by adversarial narrative topic,
such as anti-immigrant, misogyny, anti-vax, etc., which is useful
and compelling for brands.

Antitrust Enforcement
Right now,the digital ad tech market is dominated by
two companies, Facebook and Google. Advertisers
from around the world pav on average two thirds of
their budget to just these two companies.
Yet advertisers have little to no say over where their
ads are appearing. When the advertisers complain-
as many did last summer as part of the
#StopHateForProfit campaign—these companies
simply defy them. They have little incentive to better
serve their customers by blocking ads-and
funding—to sites peddling disinformation and hate.
Privacy Regulation
Personal data is the fuel that powers the algorithmic
distortion engine that is modern social media, which
at this point is creating a personalized, warped reality
for each individual among over half the world's
population.
But targeted advertising has also robbed traditional
media outlets of their primary asset: Their audience.
This effect has devastated publisher revenues and
destroyed the business models that previously
supported quality journalism, leaving a news vacuum
that is being filled by disinformation.

Section 230 essentially makes internet platforms
immune to legal liability for both the content that
users post and the decisions they make to remove
that content. Social media recommender algorithms
shape the reality of over half the world's population.
And yet, because of a specific legal carveout created
a quarter century ago, these platforms are immune
from nearly all legal liability. Their algorithms can
recommend users join white supremacist groups,
amplify conspiracy theories, promote eating disorders
to teen girls, and even inspire genocide, yet they
remain legally immune.

"Information Disorder and Its Threat to Democracy"
The Office of Security (SEC) and Bureau for Development, Democracy and Innovation, Center for
Democracy, Human Rights and Governance (DDI/DRG) invites you to join us for a discussion on mis- dis-
and mal-information and its threat to democracy with Dr. Daniel Rogers, the Co-Founder and Executive
Director at the Global Disinformation Index, an NGO that aims to catalyze change in the tech industry to
disincentivize the creation and dissemination of online disinformation.
Dr. Rogers is a physicist, an author, and an expert in cryptography, cybercrime, disinformation, and security.
He currently teaches in the Cybercrime and Global Security Masters Program at New York University and
serves as a Technical Advisor for the United Nations Development Programme. His presentation will
highlight the complexities of defining disinformation and discuss tangible ways to counter it.
This presentation is co-sponsored by DDI/DRG, which recently released USAID's Disinformation Primer,
and is part of the quarterly SEC Guest Speaker Series which aims to help all USAID staff better understand
security-related issues impacting our work.
